name: Why a Teacher Reads First
title: Why a Teacher Reads First
answer: Before students see any AI output that describes people, events, or cultures, a teacher should read it first. AI tools learn from human writing and carry its blind spots, so their descriptions can stereotype groups, omit perspectives, or present one side of a contested issue as settled. The teacher's quick review catches these problems and can turn them into a lesson on reading sources critically.

crumbs.name: Social Studies, Civics, and World Languages

sections.body: This idea says that any AI tool producing perspectives, summaries, or historical content must be checked by a teacher before it reaches students. The problem it solves is bias: AI learns from huge amounts of human text, and that text carries the blind spots of its authors. A tool might describe a group in stereotyped terms, leave a group out, or treat one side of a debate as fact. In social studies this matters most, because biased output can shape how students understand whole peoples and events, and students may not notice when the text sounds authoritative.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a social studies classroom, a teacher reads the tool's output before assigning it, looking for stereotypes, missing perspectives, one sided framing, and claims that need checking. The review does not need to be long, and Figure 9.4 lists what to look for. When the teacher finds a problem, it can become a lesson in itself, teaching students to read AI output with the same care they bring to any source. The text gives this guidance for social studies, civics, and world languages rather than by grade band. The same habit applies wherever a tool produces perspectives, summaries, or historical content.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this idea as practice based rather than research based. Its supporting example comes from Chapter 1, which described how bias in AI detectors wrongly flagged writing by students learning English (Liang et al., 2023). The text offers no study or figure of its own for the teacher review step beyond Figure 9.4, which lists what to look for. So the case for reading first rests on the known problem of bias in AI output and on professional practice, not on a dedicated study of the review routine itself.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits are clear: AI output about people, cultures, and contested events can be wrong or one sided, and students may accept it because it sounds authoritative. The teacher's review is the safeguard, and it stays with a person, not the tool. The decisions about what students read, what counts as a problem, and when a flaw becomes a lesson all remain with the teacher. The text does not ask teachers to block AI, only to read its output first and to treat it like any other source that needs checking.
